title: When did a stranger change your life?
author: Thomson, Jonny
summary: Jonny Thomson describes a spontaneous extended conversation with an elderly woman in a village cafe—she shared that her daughter had died of cancer at nine years old—and uses the moment to explore the Japanese concept of ichigo ichie: 'one meeting, one opportunity.' The 13th-century Zen master Dogen's insight that impermanence is not something to fear but the condition that makes any moment precious gives the essay its philosophical spine. Thomson introduces 'pre-emptive grief'—sadness felt now for the future loss of something present—and applies it to parenting young children: the eldest is getting heavy, it's getting harder, he won't be able to carry him forever. The essay argues that the right response to impermanence is not denial of future loss but a reframe: let the weight of future loss add to the present joy rather than diminish it. The coin metaphor (heads: polite and curt; tails: lean back and ask a follow-up question) captures the habitual openness that makes these encounters possible.
points: Openness to strangers is a practice, not an accident. At moments when a conversation could go either way, Thomson describes hearing a coin spin in his mind—heads: give a polite but curt response; tails: smile, lean back, and ask a follow-up question. It almost always lands on tails. That disposition is a cultivated habit, not a character trait.

Ichigo ichie—one meeting, one opportunity—is not just a concept for tea ceremonies. It is an attitude toward every encounter: this exact configuration of mood, light, and tone will never happen again, not like that. Treating each moment as once-in-a-lifetime is both accurate and a way of entering it fully.

Pre-emptive grief is not a failure of emotional regulation but an honest response to time. Trying to deny it produces nothing useful; the better move is to reframe: let the future loss add to the present joy. The cherry blossom is beautiful precisely because it is brief.
quotes: I can hear a coin spinning in my mind. Heads: give a polite but curt response. You've got work to do. Tails: smile, lean back, and ask a follow-up question. It almost always lands on tails.
I recognized that the encounter — that moment, that exact configuration of mood and light and tone — will never happen again. Not like that.
If the cherry blossoms lasted forever, nobody would travel to see them.
The universe has presented me and only me with this moment. And that's the most special thing the universe can give.

It's silly to let future pain ruin present joy, but it's sillier to try to deny emotions. The best I can do is reframe what is going on. I can try to savor the uniqueness of now and let the future loss add to the present joy.
